{{Short description|Infinite sum of sines and cosines}}
{{about|the mathematical concept|the book by Zygmund|Trigonometric Series}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2019}}
{{Trigonometry}}

In [[mathematics]], '''trigonometric series'''  are a special class of [[Orthogonality_(mathematics)|orthogonal]] [[series (mathematics)|series]] of the form{{sfn|Hardy|Rogosinski|1999|pp=2,4}}{{sfn|Zygmund|1968|pp=6-7}}

: <math> A_0 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty A_n \cos{(nx)} + B_n \sin{(nx)},</math>

where <math>x</math> is the variable and <math>\{A_n\}</math> and <math>\{B_n\}</math> are [[coefficient]]s. It is an infinite version of a [[trigonometric polynomial]].

A trigonometric series is called the [[Fourier series]] of the [[integrable function]] <math display=inline>f</math> if the coefficients have the form:

:<math>A_n=\frac1\pi \int^{2 \pi}_0\! f(x) \cos{(nx)} \,dx</math>

:<math>B_n=\frac{1}{\pi}\displaystyle\int^{2 \pi}_0\! f(x) \sin{(nx)} \, dx</math>

== Examples ==
[[File:Fourier series for the identity function.png|thumb|The Fourier series for the identity function suffers from the [[Gibbs phenomenon]] near the ends of the periodic interval.]]
Every Fourier series gives an example of a trigonometric series.
Let the function <math>f(x) = x</math> on <math>[-\pi,\pi]</math> be extended periodically (see [[sawtooth wave]]).  Then its Fourier coefficients are:
:<math>\begin{align}
A_n &= \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} x \cos{(nx)} \,dx = 0, \quad n \ge 0. \\[4pt]
B_n &= \frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} x \sin{(nx)} \, dx \\[4pt]
&= -\frac{x}{n\pi} \cos{(nx)} + \frac1{n^2\pi}\sin{(nx)} \Bigg\vert_{x=-\pi}^\pi \\[5mu]
&= \frac{2\,(-1)^{n+1}}{n}, \quad n \ge 1.\end{align}</math>
Which gives an example of a trigonometric series:
:<math>2\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n} \sin{(nx)} = 2\sin{(x)} - \frac22\sin{(2x)} + \frac23\sin{(3x)} - \frac24\sin{(4x) } + \cdots</math>

[[File:Trigonometric series with wiggles and spike.png|thumb|The trigonometric series {{math|sin 2''x''&thinsp;/&thinsp;log 2}} {{math|+ sin 3''x''&thinsp;/&thinsp;log 3}} {{math|+ sin 4''x''&thinsp;/&thinsp;log 4 + ...}} is not a Fourier series.]]
However, the converse is false. For example,
:<math>\sum_{n=2}^\infty \frac{\sin{(nx)}}{\log{n}} = \frac{\sin{(2x)}}{\log{2}} + \frac{\sin{(3x)}}{\log{3}} + \frac{\sin{( 4x)}}{\log{4}}+\cdots</math>
is a trigonometric series which converges for all <math>x</math> but is not a [[Fourier series]].{{sfn|Edwards|1979|pp=158-159}}{{sfn|Edwards|1982|pp=95-96}}

==Uniqueness of trigonometric series==
The uniqueness and the zeros of trigonometric series was an active area of research in 19th century Europe. First, [[Georg Cantor]] proved that if a trigonometric series is convergent to a function <math>f</math> on the interval <math>[0, 2\pi]</math>, which is identically zero, or more generally, is nonzero on at most finitely many points, then the coefficients of the series are all zero.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.math.caltech.edu/papers/uniqueness.pdf|title=Set theory and uniqueness for trigonometric series|first=Alexander S.|last=Kechris|publisher=Caltech|year=1997}}</ref>

Later Cantor proved that even if the set ''S'' on which <math>f</math> is nonzero is infinite, but the [[Derived set (mathematics)|derived set]] ''S''' of ''S'' is finite, then the coefficients are all zero. In fact, he proved a more general result. Let ''S''<sub>''0''</sub> = ''S'' and let ''S''<sub>''k+1''</sub> be the [[Derived set (mathematics)|derived set]] of ''S''<sub>''k''</sub>. If there is a finite number ''n'' for which ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> is finite, then all the coefficients are zero. Later, Lebesgue proved that if there is a countably infinite [[Ordinal number|ordinal]] ''α'' such that ''S''<sub>''α''</sub> is finite, then the coefficients of the series are all zero. Cantor's work on the uniqueness problem famously led him to invent [[transfinite number|transfinite]] [[ordinal numbers]], which appeared as the subscripts ''α'' in ''S''<sub>''α''</sub> .<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cooke|first1=Roger|title=Uniqueness of trigonometric series and descriptive set theory, 1870–1985|journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences|volume=45|pages=281–334|year=1993|doi=10.1007/BF01886630|issue=4|s2cid=122744778 |postscript=.}}</ref>
